study_material.title: Supply Chain Fundamentals
study_material.introduction: A supply chain is the network of organizations, people, activities and resources involved in moving a product from raw material to the end customer. Operations interviews test whether you can map this flow, identify where value (and cost) is added, and reason about trade-offs like cost vs. speed vs. reliability.
learning_objectives: Describe the end-to-end flow: suppliers, manufacturing, distribution, retail, customer
Distinguish push vs. pull supply chains and when each fits
Explain the bullwhip effect and what causes it
Compare centralized vs. decentralized distribution models
Use basic SCM vocabulary correctly: lead time, fill rate, SKU, 3PL

concepts.heading: 1. The End-to-End Flow
concepts.body: Raw materials -> suppliers -> manufacturing/production -> warehousing -> distribution -> retail/last mile -> customer. Each handoff adds lead time and cost, and each stage holds inventory as a buffer against variability. In interviews, always start by sketching this flow for the specific product in question before jumping to solutions.

concepts.heading: 2. Push vs. Pull Systems
concepts.body: Push systems produce based on forecasts and push inventory downstream (good for stable, predictable demand - e.g. commodities). Pull systems produce/replenish only in response to actual demand signals (good for volatile demand or high holding cost - e.g. fashion, perishables). Most real chains are hybrid: push upstream (bulk raw materials) and pull downstream (final assembly to order).

concepts.heading: 3. The Bullwhip Effect
concepts.body: Small fluctuations in real customer demand get amplified into larger swings as you move upstream through the chain, because each stage adds its own buffer/safety margin when forecasting from the stage below it rather than from true end demand. Causes: demand-signal processing, order batching, price fluctuations (promotions), and rationing/shortage gaming. Fixes: share point-of-sale data upstream, smaller/more frequent orders, stable pricing, vendor-managed inventory.

concepts.heading: 4. Distribution Network Design
concepts.body: Centralized (one large warehouse) minimizes total inventory (risk pooling) and cost but increases delivery lead time. Decentralized (many regional warehouses) does the opposite - faster delivery, higher total safety stock needed. The right answer depends on product value density, demand variability by region, and customer service targets.

formulas: Lead time = order placement to order receipt (supplier lead time + transit time + processing time)
Fill rate = orders fulfilled from stock on hand / total orders placed
Perfect order rate = % of orders delivered complete, on time, undamaged, with correct documentation
shortcut_methods: In case interviews, always draw the flow diagram first - it forces you to locate the actual bottleneck instead of guessing
When asked 'should we centralize or decentralize', anchor on: demand variability (favors centralize), delivery speed requirement (favors decentralize)
If demand is unpredictable, default recommendation is pull + smaller batches + more frequent replenishment, not more forecasting
common_mistakes: Treating 'supply chain' and 'logistics' as synonyms - logistics (transport/warehousing) is one part of the broader supply chain (which also includes sourcing, production planning, and demand planning)
Recommending more forecasting accuracy as the fix for bullwhip effect instead of fixing information sharing and batching
Assuming centralization is always cheaper - it's cheaper in inventory holding but adds transportation cost and delivery time
study_material.summary: Supply chain questions are really about trade-offs: cost vs. speed, centralization vs. responsiveness, forecast-driven vs. demand-driven. Map the flow, name the trade-off explicitly, then make a reasoned call.
quick_revision_notes: Push = forecast-driven, Pull = demand-driven, most chains are hybrid
Bullwhip effect: demand variability amplifies upstream - fix with shared data, not more forecasting
Centralize = lower inventory cost, slower delivery; Decentralize = opposite
Fill rate and perfect order rate are the standard customer-service metrics

practice_questions.question: Which of these best describes a 'pull' supply chain system?
options: Production is triggered by actual customer demand signals
Production is based purely on long-range sales forecasts
Inventory is held only at the manufacturing site
All orders are batched monthly regardless of demand
practice_questions.correct_answer: Production is triggered by actual customer demand signals
practice_questions.explanation: Pull systems replenish/produce in response to real demand rather than forecasts, reducing excess inventory risk.

practice_questions.question: The bullwhip effect refers to:
options: Amplification of demand variability as you move upstream in the supply chain
A sudden drop in transportation costs
The tendency of retailers to under-order during promotions
A method for calculating safety stock
practice_questions.correct_answer: Amplification of demand variability as you move upstream in the supply chain
practice_questions.explanation: Small changes in end-customer demand get magnified into large swings for upstream suppliers due to batching, forecasting lag, and order gaming.

practice_questions.question: A company centralizes its warehouse from 10 regional locations into 1 national facility. What is the most likely trade-off?
options: Lower total inventory cost, but longer delivery times to customers
Higher total inventory cost, and longer delivery times
Lower total inventory cost, and shorter delivery times
No change in cost or delivery time
practice_questions.correct_answer: Lower total inventory cost, but longer delivery times to customers
practice_questions.explanation: Centralization pools risk/safety stock (lower total inventory) but customers are now farther from the warehouse on average, increasing delivery time.

practice_questions.question: Fill rate measures:
options: The proportion of demand met directly from available stock
The cost of holding one unit of inventory for a year
The number of SKUs a warehouse carries
The speed of a delivery truck
practice_questions.correct_answer: The proportion of demand met directly from available stock
practice_questions.explanation: Fill rate = orders/units fulfilled from on-hand stock, divided by total demand - a core customer-service metric.

practice_questions.question: A fashion retailer with highly unpredictable, fast-changing demand is currently forecasting 6 months ahead and pushing inventory to stores. What is the single most impactful change to recommend?
options: Shift toward a pull-based, shorter replenishment cycle closer to actual demand
Increase the forecast horizon to 12 months for more data
Centralize all production in one factory regardless of location
Increase safety stock at every store to avoid stockouts
practice_questions.correct_answer: Shift toward a pull-based, shorter replenishment cycle closer to actual demand
practice_questions.explanation: For volatile, fast-fashion demand, forecast accuracy degrades quickly over long horizons - the standard fix is to move closer to a pull system with shorter cycles (like fast-fashion players do), not to forecast further out or just add more stock.
